name: System design: caching, hashing, databases, Kafka
description: How the pieces of backend systems work and trade off.

cards.front: Cache-aside (lazy loading): who loads data into the cache?
cards.back: The application: on a miss it reads the database, then writes the result into the cache.

cards.front: Write-through vs. write-back caching
cards.back: Write-through writes the cache and the database together (safe, slower writes). Write-back writes the cache first and flushes to the database later (fast, can lose data on a crash).

cards.front: What is a cache stampede (thundering herd)?
cards.back: A hot key expires and many requests miss at once, all hitting the database together.

cards.front: Three ways to prevent a cache stampede
cards.back: Request coalescing (one request recomputes, others wait), a lock or lease per key, and early probabilistic refresh / jittered TTLs.

cards.front: Why add random jitter to cache TTLs?
cards.back: So keys written together don't all expire together and cause a burst of misses.

cards.front: LRU vs. LFU eviction
cards.back: LRU evicts what was used longest ago; LFU evicts what is used least often. LFU keeps steady favorites; LRU adapts faster to new patterns.

cards.front: Which eviction policy fits a scan-heavy workload that would flush an LRU cache?
cards.back: A scan-resistant policy such as LFU, ARC, or segmented LRU (or 2Q / W-TinyLFU).

cards.front: What does a CDN cache, and where?
cards.back: Static (and some dynamic) responses at edge servers near users, cutting latency and origin load.

cards.front: What is negative caching?
cards.back: Caching 'not found' results so repeated lookups for missing keys don't hit the database.

cards.front: Hardest part of caching, per the classic joke?
cards.back: Cache invalidation (and naming things, and off-by-one errors).

cards.front: Redis vs. Memcached: which supports data structures, persistence and replication?
cards.back: Redis

cards.front: Problem with hash(key) mod N for sharding
cards.back: When N changes, almost every key moves to a different server.

cards.front: Consistent hashing in one sentence
cards.back: Servers and keys sit on a hash ring; each key goes to the next server clockwise, so adding or removing a server moves only about 1/N of keys.

cards.front: Why use virtual nodes in consistent hashing?
cards.back: Each server gets many points on the ring, which evens out load and spreads a failed server's keys across many others.

cards.front: What is rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing?
cards.back: For each key, score every server with hash(key, server) and pick the highest. Like consistent hashing, few keys move when servers change.

cards.front: What does a Bloom filter answer, and what errors can it make?
cards.back: 'Is X possibly in the set?' It can give false positives but never false negatives.

cards.front: Why can't you delete from a standard Bloom filter?
cards.back: Clearing a bit might also remove other items that set it. A counting Bloom filter fixes this.

cards.front: What is HyperLogLog used for?
cards.back: Estimating the number of distinct items (cardinality) using a tiny, fixed amount of memory.

cards.front: What does a count-min sketch estimate?
cards.back: How often items appear in a stream (frequencies), possibly overestimating, never underestimating.

cards.front: Cryptographic vs. non-cryptographic hash: which for a hash table?
cards.back: Non-cryptographic (e.g. MurmurHash, xxHash): much faster, and collision resistance against attackers isn't needed.

cards.front: Why store passwords with bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 instead of SHA-256?
cards.back: They're deliberately slow and salted, which makes brute-force and rainbow-table attacks expensive.

cards.front: ACID stands for…
cards.back: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

cards.front: Read committed vs. repeatable read
cards.back: Read committed only shows committed data but a re-read can change. Repeatable read keeps rows you've read stable for the whole transaction.

cards.front: What anomaly does serializable isolation prevent that snapshot isolation allows?
cards.back: Write skew: two transactions read overlapping data and write different rows, breaking a rule neither saw broken.
choices: Lost updates on the same row

cards.front: What is MVCC?
cards.back: Multi-version concurrency control: writers create new row versions so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking.

cards.front: B-tree vs. LSM-tree: which favors write-heavy workloads?
cards.back: LSM-tree (buffers writes in memory, flushes sorted files, compacts later).

cards.front: What is write amplification in an LSM-tree?
cards.back: Each logical write is rewritten several times during compaction, so disk writes exceed app writes.

cards.front: What is a covering index?
cards.back: An index containing every column a query needs, so the database never has to read the table rows.

cards.front: Composite index on (a, b): can it serve a filter on b alone?
cards.back: Usually not efficiently. Composite indexes work left to right (leftmost prefix).

cards.front: Leader-follower replication: what is replication lag's classic user-facing bug?
cards.back: You write, then read from a stale follower and your own change seems missing. Fix with read-your-writes routing.

cards.front: Synchronous vs. asynchronous replication trade-off
cards.back: Synchronous never loses acknowledged writes but adds latency and stalls on slow replicas. Async is fast but can lose recent writes on failover.

cards.front: What does a quorum of W + R > N guarantee?
cards.back: Every read overlaps at least one replica holding the latest write.

cards.front: CAP theorem in practice
cards.back: During a network partition, a system must choose between consistency and availability.

cards.front: What does PACELC add to CAP?
cards.back: Else (no partition), there's still a trade-off between latency and consistency.

cards.front: Range vs. hash partitioning
cards.back: Range keeps neighbors together (good scans, risk of hot spots). Hash spreads load evenly but range scans hit every shard.

cards.front: What's a hot partition, and a common fix?
cards.back: One shard gets far more traffic than others. Fix by salting/splitting the hot key or choosing a better partition key.

cards.front: Two-phase commit's big weakness
cards.back: If the coordinator dies after 'prepare', participants can block holding locks until it recovers.

cards.front: What is the outbox pattern?
cards.back: Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the data, then a relay publishes it. No dual-write inconsistency.

cards.front: Kafka: what is the unit of parallelism and ordering?
cards.back: The partition. Order is guaranteed only within a partition.

cards.front: How does Kafka decide a message's partition?
cards.back: Hash of the message key (same key → same partition), or round-robin/sticky if there's no key.

cards.front: Consumer group rule: max useful consumers for a topic with 6 partitions?
cards.back: 6. Each partition goes to one consumer in the group; extras sit idle.

cards.front: What is a consumer offset?
cards.back: The position of the next message to read in a partition, committed so a consumer can resume after a restart.

cards.front: acks=all in a Kafka producer means…
cards.back: The leader waits for all in-sync replicas to have the write before acknowledging.

cards.front: What does min.insync.replicas protect against?
cards.back: With acks=all, writes fail unless at least that many replicas are in sync, preventing silent data loss.

cards.front: At-least-once vs. at-most-once delivery
cards.back: At-least-once commits offsets after processing (may duplicate). At-most-once commits before (may lose).

cards.front: How do you get effectively-once processing with at-least-once delivery?
cards.back: Make the consumer idempotent, e.g. dedupe by message ID or use upserts. Kafka also has idempotent producers and transactions.

cards.front: What is log compaction in Kafka?
cards.back: Kafka keeps at least the latest value for each key and drops older ones, turning a topic into a durable changelog.

cards.front: Kafka vs. a traditional queue (e.g. RabbitMQ): biggest model difference
cards.back: Kafka is a replayable log that consumers read at their own offsets. A queue removes messages once acknowledged.

cards.front: What is a dead-letter queue?
cards.back: Where messages that repeatedly fail processing go, so they don't block the rest.

cards.front: What is backpressure?
cards.back: A slow consumer signals producers to slow down (or buffers fill), instead of being overwhelmed.

cards.front: Rate limiting: token bucket in one line
cards.back: Tokens refill at a steady rate up to a cap; each request spends one, which allows short bursts.

cards.front: Why use exponential backoff with jitter on retries?
cards.back: Spreads retries out so many clients don't retry in lockstep and swamp a recovering service.

cards.front: What is a circuit breaker?
cards.back: After repeated failures it stops calling a dependency for a while and fails fast, then tests with a few calls before closing.

cards.front: What is an idempotency key?
cards.back: A client-supplied ID so a retried request (like a payment) is applied only once.

cards.front: p99 latency means…
cards.back: 99% of requests are faster than this. It reflects the slowest 1% that averages hide.
